title: The Foot-in-the-Door Technique: Does It Work?
voiceover: Can a tiny request make you say yes to a bigger one? Researchers Freedman and Fraser tested what they called the foot-in-the-door technique in 1966. They asked homeowners in Palo Alto, California, to agree to a small request first. In one experiment, 53 percent agreed to a two-hour home visit by investigators after a small earlier request. Without that first small request, only 22 percent agreed. The authors suggested agreeing changes how you see yourself: as the kind of person who helps. But in a 1984 meta-analysis, Dillard, Hunter and Burgoon found the effect was small, with a correlation of about 0.17. It worked mainly when the request was prosocial, such as helping a cause. So a small yes can nudge a bigger one, but the effect is modest. Tomorrow: why does a short silence feel so awkward?

But in a 1984 meta-analysis, Dillard, Hunter and Burgoon found the effect was small, with a correlation of about 0.17.
It worked mainly when the request was prosocial, such as helping a cause.

description: Does agreeing to a small request make you say yes to a bigger one? In a 1966 field experiment it did, but a 1984 meta-analysis found the effect small. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Freedman, J. L., & Fraser, S. C. (1966). Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 4(2), 195-202. Source: Dillard, J. P., Hunter, J. E., & Burgoon, M. (1984). Sequential-request persuasive strategies: Meta-analysis of foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face. Human Communication Research, 10(4), 461-488.
accuracy_note: The 53% vs 22% figures come from secondary summaries of Freedman & Fraser (1966). Dillard et al. (1984) found a small average effect (r about .17) that depended on request type (stronger when prosocial). The video states both the original effect and its modest size.
